title: The Sarkar-e-Khalsa
hookLine: crowned Maharaja, he calls his government the Khalsa's and strikes coins in the Gurus' names

lines: A NEW KING, A NEW NAME.
cards: A ruler holds the great city of the Punjab, and a new king has a question to answer: what's this called, and whose is it? The usual answer is a family name: my house, my throne, my reign, the coins carrying my face.
Ranjit Singh takes the title Maharaja. And then, by the histories' account, he does something odd with it. He gives the credit away.

teach.b: Sarkar-e-Khalsa means, roughly, the government of the Khalsa. Not of Ranjit Singh.
The state, in its own name, belonged to the Khalsa, the community Guru Gobind Singh had founded, and the Maharaja was its servant, at least in the way it spoke of itself.
Next, the coins. A ruler's coins are a loud announcement, passing from hand to hand across the land. Ranjit Singh's coins did not carry his own name or face.

They carried a Persian verse giving the victory to Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, a verse Sikhs had used on coins and seals before him. The money said, in effect: everything here was given by the Gurus.

Then the throne. Tradition says he was reluctant to sit high, and liked to hold court sitting cross-legged on a chair or among his chiefs, and that people called him simply Sarkar, more readily than any grand title.
None of this means he was shy of power; he held a great deal of it.
But the way the kingdom named itself kept pointing past the king.
It echoes the misl years, when bands of equals decided before the Guru, even as those bands gave way to one ruler. Some historians say it was faith, some wise politics, some both.
Either way, the message was on every coin in every market.

how: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's state as the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government of the Khalsa, and his coins, known as Nanakshahi coins, carried a verse in the names of the Gurus rather than his own.

practice: Think of shared work where your part was the one people saw, a project, a family event, a team win, and find the part nobody praised: who set up the chairs, checked the numbers, washed the pots?
Pick one of them and shape a single plain sentence you could say about what they did, in front of others; if you pray, breathe Waheguru as you go.

wordCard.voice: The Sarkar-e-Khalsa. The government of the Khalsa, with coins in the Gurus' names. This week: Rani Sada Kaur, a boy of twelve, the misls close, born at Gujranwala, leading at twelve, Lahore, and the Sarkar-e-Khalsa. Today's word.
